subject: Business Models
title: Multi-Sided Platforms
description: A quick, practical guide to Multi-Sided Platforms.

hook.text: Facebook serves users, advertisers, app developers, and publishers. That's four sides, not two.

buildup.text: Each additional side creates new value exchanges. More sides mean more revenue streams.

discovery.text: Amazon serves buyers, sellers, advertisers, AWS developers, and delivery partners. Five sides, one platform.

twist.text: Managing multiple sides creates conflicts. Amazon both hosts sellers and competes with them.

climax.text: Multi-sided platforms are harder to build but create deeper moats once established.

punchline.text: More sides, more moats, more conflicts. Complexity pays.

quiz.question: What challenge do multi-sided platforms face?

details.summary: Multi-sided platforms serve three or more distinct user groups simultaneously, with each group benefiting from the others' participation. Google connects users, advertisers, and content publishers. Amazon connects buyers, sellers, and delivery partners in an interconnected ecosystem.
details.whyItMatters: The most valuable platforms serve multiple sides, not just two. Each additional side creates new value connections that strengthen the platform's position and make it harder for single-purpose competitors to displace.
takeaways: Multi-sided platforms connect three or more interdependent user groups
Each additional side creates compounding network effects across the ecosystem
Managing multiple sides requires balancing competing interests carefully

faq.question: What challenges arise from serving multiple platform sides?
faq.answer: Each side has different needs, pricing sensitivities, and expectations. Policies that benefit one side may harm another. Platform governance must balance competing interests while maintaining value for all participants and preventing any side from dominating.

faq.question: How does Amazon function as a multi-sided platform?
faq.answer: Amazon connects buyers seeking products, third-party sellers seeking customers, delivery partners seeking routes, advertisers seeking visibility, and developers using AWS. Each side reinforces the others, creating a self-reinforcing ecosystem that is extremely difficult to replicate.
